title: This Drone Perches Like a Bird, Using Touch
summary:
A flying robot can perch like a bird using touch. Researchers at Delft University of Technology in the Netherlands built it to feel its way onto a branch and hang there without using extra energy.

Perching could let drones stay in one place for a long time, to watch over factories and power lines or study wildlife. But gripping well has been tricky: cameras can be blocked in crowded places.

It uses touch instead of sight. It has three fingers: a thumb, a pointer finger, and a middle finger. Each finger has three parts, called phalanges, with touch sensors on soft silicone pads.

Springs keep the fingers closed, like a clothespin, so it can hang on without spending more energy. A motor pulls metal cords, like the tendons in human fingers, to open them before landing.

The team, led by roboticist Anton Bredenbeck, wanted a drone that could stay in fragile places to study them. Bredenbeck says drones are inefficient flyers. Cecilia Laschi, who did not work on the project, called it a good example of embodied intelligence.
why_it_matters: It shows how copying nature can help robots do useful jobs, like watching wildlife without disturbing it.

keywords.explanation: To perch means to sit or rest on a branch, like a bird does.
Phalanges are the small bones that make up fingers.
Silicone is a soft, bendy material a bit like rubber.
Tendons are strong cords in the body that pull on bones to move fingers.
A roboticist is a person who designs and builds robots.

background_read: A drone is a flying robot that can fly without a person inside it.
Birds perch by gripping a branch with their feet, which lets them rest in one place without flying.
This drone copies that idea, using touch to feel its way onto a branch and hold on while it stays still.
